claims.claim: Sustainability is commonly divided into three dimensions, environmental, economic, and social, popularly shortened to people, planet, and profit.

The UN 2030 Agenda (resolution A/RES/70/1, adopted 25 September 2015) commits to sustainable development in its three dimensions, economic, social and environmental, in a balanced and integrated manner.

John Elkington coined the phrase 'triple bottom line' in 1994, arguing business performance should be measured on economic, environmental, and social fronts, and the shorthand 'people, planet, profit' derives from this work.

In a 2018 Harvard Business Review article (published 25 June 2018) Elkington called for a 'recall' / rethink of the triple bottom line, arguing it had been reduced to an accounting and box-ticking exercise rather than provoking systemic change as he intended.

Purvis, Mao & Robinson (2019) found no single point of origin for the three-pillar model; it emerged gradually, the popular three-circles diagram was first presented by Barbier (1987), and they found nowhere a theoretically rigorous description of the three pillars.

The three dimensions are drawn in two competing ways: three overlapping circles with sustainability at the central intersection, and a nested model with the economy inside society inside the environment.

Weak sustainability (associated with neoclassical/environmental economics and Solow, Hartwick, Pearce) holds that human-made capital can substitute for natural capital, while strong sustainability (associated with ecological economics and Herman Daly) holds that critical natural capital is non-substitutable and must be preserved; the debate is unresolved.

The EPA frames sustainability around the interdependence of people and nature, stating that everything people need for survival and well-being depends, directly or indirectly, on the natural environment, and that the goal is conditions under which humans and nature exist in productive harmony for present and future generations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether human-made capital can substitute for natural capital (weak vs strong sustainability).
positions: Weak sustainability: substitution is generally acceptable if total capital does not decline (Solow, Hartwick, Pearce; neoclassical/environmental economics).
Strong sustainability: critical natural capital provides non-substitutable life-support functions and must be maintained in its own right (Daly; ecological economics).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuine, unresolved debate; the lesson attributes each position and adjudicates neither.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which visual model of the three dimensions is correct: equal overlapping circles or nested layers.
positions: Overlapping circles: the three dimensions are roughly equal and independent.
Nested model: the environment is the outer bound on society and economy (aligns with strong sustainability).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both models are described; the lesson notes the drawing encodes a worldview and does not declare one correct.

sourceRecords.title: Three pillars of sustainability: in search of conceptual origins
sourceRecords.provider: Sustainability Science (Springer); authors Ben Purvis, Yong Mao, Darren Robinson
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read from the White Rose Research Online published-version PDF (https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/136715/7/Purvis2018_Article_ThreePillarsOfSustainabilityIn.pdf); canonical DOI recorded in url. Sustainability Science 14(3):681-695, 2019, CC BY. Abstract confirms: no single point of origin for the three-pillar conception; gradual emergence; three-circles diagram first presented by Barbier (1987); 'nowhere have we found a theoretically rigorous description of the three pillars.' Used for origins, the three-circles model, and the lack of rigorous theory.

sourceRecords.title: 25 Years Ago I Coined the Phrase 'Triple Bottom Line.' Here's Why It's Time to Rethink It
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard Business Review; author John Elkington
sourceRecords.notes: Verified via WebFetch (published 25 June 2018). Confirms Elkington coined 'triple bottom line' in 1994 and, 25 years on, called for a 'recall' of the concept, asking how often inventors recall their own management ideas; his argument is that the TBL had been flattened into accounting/box-ticking rather than driving systemic change. Copyrighted; reference-only, no substantial quotation.

sourceRecords.title: Weak and strong sustainability (overview of natural-capital substitutability debate)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier-D secondary source used only to corroborate standard, textbook attributions: weak sustainability (substitutable natural capital) to neoclassical/environmental economics and Solow, Hartwick, Pearce; strong sustainability (non-substitutable critical natural capital) to ecological economics and Herman Daly; and the nested model as the visual expression of strong sustainability. The named-scholar attributions are well-established in the field; no wording reproduced.
